analysis.one_liner: Removes the liability cap so offshore oil companies pay the full cost of spills.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after being referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee in April 2013, it sat in a subcommittee until Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, a company responsible for an offshore oil spill pays cleanup costs plus up to $75 million in damages, leaving taxpayers and spill victims to cover costs beyond that. This bill would strike that cap, making the responsible company pay everything. It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Coast Guard subcommittee on April 25-26, 2013, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, fishing and tourism businesses, and taxpayers. If a spill costs more than $75 million in damages, those costs currently fall on victims and, in the worst case, on the public; this bill would put the full bill on the company that caused the spill.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the $75 million limit on a responsible party's liability for oil discharged from an offshore facility, so companies pay the full cost of spills they cause.
The bill's stated purpose is to require responsible parties to pay the full cost of offshore oil spills, titled the Big Oil Bailout Prevention Act of 2013.
Victims of a major spill — fishermen, coastal businesses, shoreline property owners — would no longer have their compensation cut off at the statutory cap.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would face unlimited financial liability for spills from their offshore facilities. The risk of catastrophic losses like a Deepwater Horizon-style disaster would sit with drillers and their insurers rather than the public.

drawbacks.text: Unlimited liability raises the financial risk of offshore drilling, which could push some operators — particularly smaller companies without large balance sheets — out of deepwater projects or raise drilling costs that get passed through energy prices.

The bill does not touch the parallel cap for deepwater ports, so liability rules remain different for that class of facility, and critics of unlimited liability argue uncapped damages can be unpredictable for insuring and financing offshore operations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: shifting catastrophic spill risk from victims and taxpayers to the companies that profit from offshore drilling. The cost side is real but indirect — higher perceived risk and insurance costs for offshore operations, and possibly less drilling — while the benefit side protects ordinary people from footing cleanup and compensation bills for someone else's disaster. The bill does nothing to change liability for deepwater ports, a narrow gap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rush Holt introduced the bill on April 25, 2013, joined by six Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Grijalva, Castor, Slaughter, Capps, Polis, and Markey.
The same day it was introduced, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
On April 26, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, and that is where the record ends.
No committee action, no vote, and no floor consideration ever occurred in the 113th Congress, and the bill died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas companies are better off: the $75 million liability cap that limits what they must pay after a catastrophic spill stays in place, and the risk of costs above that cap remains with spill victims and the public.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil companies keep the liability cap

for.name: Rep. Rush Holt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Big Oil Bailout Prevention Act of 2013 to remove the offshore spill liability cap.

for.name: Reps. Grijalva, Castor, Slaughter, Capps, Polis, and Markey
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, bringing total support to 8 House members, all Democrats.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 113th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee on April 26, 2013, and never brought it to a markup or vote; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
against.role: Regulated industry benefiting from the existing $75 million liability cap
against.what_they_did: The bill would have exposed it to unlimited liability for offshore spills; it remained capped, and the bill received no Republican cosponsorship or committee action.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the House was under Republican control during the 113th Congress, and the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral.

industries.note: The bill would have made them pay unlimited damages for offshore spills instead of the current cap at cleanup costs plus $75 million. Its death preserves the cap, keeping spill costs above that limit on victims and taxpayers.
These businesses absorb spill losses when compensation is capped; full liability from the responsible party would better cover their damages after a spill. The bill died, so the cap remains.

Unlimited liability would have sharply raised the cost of underwriting offshore operators; the bill's death keeps their exposure limited, which lowers their risk but leaves spill costs with the public side.
